title: Blanket Fort Story Dialogue Card Pack
audience: Families, homeschool groups, tutors, and adult-led writing tables for writers ages 7-11.
sessionLength: 16 printable dialogue cards plus adult guide tools, dialogue routines, take-home dialogue slips, and optional share prompts
safetyNote: No scary harm, no bullying, no romance, no weapons, no branded characters, no real child profiles.

cover.headline: Blanket Fort Story Dialogue Card Pack
cover.subhead: Sixteen paper cards help writers draft two fictional speaker lines inside a pretend blanket-fort story scene.

beforeSession: Print the dialogue cards, blank line bubbles, turn arrows, tag strips, and take-home slips before writers arrive.
Explain that every blanket fort scene, character, place, and problem is invented for paper writing only.
Choose a small set of cozy prop cards, such as quilt flap, lantern note, pillow sign, and tunnel map.
Put pencils, erasers, and extra blank slips where the adult can hand them out without stopping the table.
Start with one adult example that shows two short lines, one tag, and one clear reply.
paperDialogueSetup: Place two character tents on the table with a turn arrow between them.
Set one setting mat under the tents so every line belongs inside the pretend fort scene.
Keep question, reply, feeling, object, and closing slips in separate paper stacks.
Use blank name tabs with role labels such as Builder, Guard, Mapper, or Visitor.
Leave a small swap pile for lines that are funny but do not fit the current scene.
dialogueCoaching: Ask what the pretend character wants before the writer fills the first line.
Point to the turn arrow and check that each new line answers or reacts to the line before it.
If two characters sound alike, invite one word change that shows a different voice.
Add simple tags only when the reader needs help knowing who speaks or how the line is said.
Read the exchange once and ask whether the fort problem moved forward.
privacyAndSafetyNotes: Keep all work on paper with the adult leader or family folder.
Use invented names, pretend roles, and made-up blanket fort places.
Turn any personal detail into a silly prop, role, or setting clue before writing.
Let a writer point, choose, or write one invented word instead of reading aloud.
Skip any prompt that stops feeling fictional, gentle, paper-only, or adult-led.
familyHandoff: Send one slip with one blank line, not a long worksheet.
Tell family adults the slip is for short invented dialogue practice at a table.
Invite one adult model line before the writer adds a reply.
Praise clear turns, voice clues, and problem-solving lines before spelling or neatness.
Return unused slips to the folder so the next adult-led session starts cleanly.
reset: Sort line bubbles, turn arrows, tag strips, setting mats, and slips into separate stacks.
Recycle scrap warm-ups and keep clean blank slips for the next table.
Clear adult examples from the table so the next group begins with fresh invented choices.
Put the blanket fort prop cards, pencils, and guide sheet back in the envelope.

dialogueRoutines.name: Fort Flap Greeting
dialogueRoutines.bestFor: Starting a scene with one friendly opening line.
steps: Adult places two pretend character tents beside the fort flap card.
Writer chooses which character speaks first.
Writer writes one greeting that fits the blanket fort setting.
Adult points to the turn arrow and asks who answers next.

dialogueRoutines.name: Question Reply Ladder
dialogueRoutines.bestFor: Writers who need help making one line connect to the next.
steps: Place a question slip above a reply slip.
Writer fills the question with a pretend fort problem or wonder.
Writer fills the reply with an answer that uses one detail from the question.
Read both lines and underline the word that connects them.

dialogueRoutines.name: Tag Tuck-In
dialogueRoutines.bestFor: Adding who said the line without cluttering the page.
steps: Writer chooses one finished line bubble.
Adult offers two short tags, such as said the Mapper or whispered the Builder.
Writer tucks the tag after the line or before the line.
Read the sentence and remove the tag if the speaker is already clear.

dialogueRoutines.name: Lantern Voice Swap
dialogueRoutines.bestFor: Revising two speakers so they sound different.
steps: Place two line bubbles under the lantern card.
Writer chooses one voice clue for each speaker, such as careful, bouncy, puzzled, or proud.
Writer changes one word in each line to match the chosen voice clue.
Adult reads the lines and asks which speaker sounds more specific.

dialogueRoutines.name: Pillow Sign Object Turn
dialogueRoutines.bestFor: Using an object to make dialogue feel grounded in the scene.
steps: Adult places one object card in the middle of the character tents.
Writer writes a line where one speaker notices or uses that object.
The next line must react to the object clue, not change the topic.
Writer circles the object word that helped the turn connect.

dialogueRoutines.name: Gentle Disagreement Fix
dialogueRoutines.bestFor: Practicing a mild difference of opinion in a fictional scene.
steps: Adult gives two characters different ideas for solving the blanket fort problem.
Writer writes one polite disagreement line for the first speaker.
Writer adds a reply that offers a compromise or new plan.
Read the two lines and check that both characters stay kind.
